title: Set Methods
learningObjectives: Explain set methods and when it is useful.
Use the relevant Python operations with correct syntax.
Predict the result of common operations and edge cases.
Distinguish mutation, return values and error behavior.
Apply the concept to a small data-processing task.

understand.concept: Set methods provide union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference, including update-in-place variants. Subset and superset tests compare membership, while isdisjoint checks for no shared elements.
understand.whyItMatters: Set Methods is useful when a program needs to organize, inspect or transform related data reliably.
understand.analogy: A set is like a collection of unique membership cards: each item is present once, with no positional promise.
understand.analogyLimit: A set does not preserve a meaningful position for each member, and elements must be hashable.

explain.narrative:
## Set Methods

Set methods provide union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference, including update-in-place variants. Subset and superset tests compare membership, while isdisjoint checks for no shared elements.

## Choosing an operation

Read the example code and check whether the operation mutates the object, returns a new value, or may raise an exception. Use membership tests and defaults where input may be missing.

## Practical reasoning

The five examples progress from basic use to a small real-world pattern. Compare each expected output with the code before changing it.

examples.expectedOutput: intersection_update retains only shared members in the original set.
difference_update removes members found in the other set.
Symmetric difference keeps values in exactly one of the sets.
The two methods express opposite directions of the same containment relation.
isdisjoint is true when the sets have no common members.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Set Methods?
options: To work with the collection using its defining operations
To convert every value to text
To sort all data automatically
To create a file
questions.answer: To work with the collection using its defining operations
questions.explanation: The lesson focuses on the stated collection behavior and its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the behavior demonstrated in example 2?
options: It uses the operation shown to produce the stated result
It always changes the original object
It raises an exception for every input
It sorts values alphabetically
questions.answer: It uses the operation shown to produce the stated result
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates the operation's result; compare it with the code and expected output.

questions.prompt: Which approach is safest when a requested item may be absent?
options: Check membership or use a documented default-returning operation
Assume the item is always present
Use an unrelated index
Catch every exception without checking
questions.answer: Check membership or use a documented default-returning operation
questions.explanation: Membership checks and default-returning methods prevent avoidable missing-item errors.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about the collection in this lesson?
options: Its operations follow the collection's documented semantics
It always preserves duplicate entries
It supports every sequence operation
Its values must all be strings
questions.answer: Its operations follow the collection's documented semantics
questions.explanation: Python collection types have distinct, documented behavior; do not assume they act like every other collection.

questions.prompt: What should a learner verify before choosing an operation?
options: Whether the operation mutates data and what it returns
Only the variable name length
Whether the editor uses dark mode
The computer's screen size
questions.answer: Whether the operation mutates data and what it returns
questions.explanation: Mutation, return values and data requirements determine whether an operation is appropriate.
